canonical_statement: The review aimed to compare cardiovascular efficacy and safety across five individual SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with type 2 diabetes and heart failure.
The review specifically sought comparative rankings for canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, ertugliflozin, and sotagliflozin.
The quantitative evidence base comprised 20,438 participants with type 2 diabetes and heart failure from 11 randomized controlled trials represented by 13 publications.

The review evaluated cardiovascular death as an outcome.
The review evaluated all-cause mortality as an outcome.
The review evaluated serious adverse events as an outcome.
The review evaluated any adverse event as an outcome.
The review was registered prospectively in PROSPERO as CRD42022353754.
PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from inception through 15 August 2022, with an update on 23 September 2022.
The search applied no language restriction.
Eligible designs were randomized controlled trials or randomized-trial subgroup/post-hoc analyses reporting outcomes for participants with both heart failure and type 2 diabetes.
Two reviewers independently performed risk-of-bias assessment using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool.
Dichotomous treatment effects were synthesized as relative risks with 95% confidence intervals.
Pairwise meta-analysis used heterogeneity statistics including Cochran Q and I-squared to select fixed- or random-effects models according to prespecified thresholds.
A two-stage network meta-analysis estimated relative treatment effects across individual SGLT2 inhibitors and standard of care.
Surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) probabilities were used to rank interventions.
Transitivity was assessed using participant, treatment, ejection-fraction, functional-class, concomitant-medication, and follow-up characteristics across network comparisons.
Comparison-adjusted funnel plots were used to assess small-study effects/publication bias.
A sensitivity analysis restricted the composite outcome network to heart-failure-specific randomized trials.
A second sensitivity analysis excluded a study with fewer than 100 participants and treatment duration under six months.
Confidence in network estimates was assessed using CINeMA with minimal clinically important differences informed by Dutch primary-care diabetes guidance.
Reviewers had 72.73% agreement on risk-of-bias judgments (kappa 0.48; p=0.03).

canonical_statement: Five of the 11 randomized trials were judged low risk of bias and six had some concerns, most often involving the randomization-process domain.

Comparison-adjusted funnel plots showed asymmetry for heart-failure hospitalization, cardiovascular death, and all-cause mortality networks, attributed to one small study with a very small effect size.
The network had no closed loop, creating major concern for incoherence and contributing to very-low-confidence CINeMA ratings for key comparative estimates.
Across 10 studies (n=20,191), pooled SGLT2 inhibitors reduced composite cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization versus standard of care (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.73-0.81).

canonical_statement: The authors reported no significant head-to-head differences among dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, and sotagliflozin in the heart-failure-specific sensitivity network.
Excluding the small CANONICAL study did not materially change the sensitivity-analysis findings.
The narrative reports follow-up spanning 0.5 to 3.6 years, whereas Table 1 lists 4.2 years for DECLARE-TIMI 58.
The narrative reports a female-percentage range beginning at 2.3%, whereas Table 1 values begin around 22.3% and include 44.36%.

The all-cause-mortality prose calls canagliflozin RR 0.76 (95% CI 0.58-1.00) significant, while Table 3 marks only the dapagliflozin estimate with its significance asterisk and the abstract says only dapagliflozin was statistically significant.

The discussion states no statistically significant associations with adverse effects or serious adverse events, while the results report significantly fewer serious adverse events for several SGLT2 inhibitors and significantly more any-adverse-event events for canagliflozin versus standard of care.
The review used aggregated study-level data rather than individual participant data, limiting adjustment for baseline confounders.
Included trials differed in patient populations, study designs, concomitant therapy, ejection fraction, and follow-up duration.
The evidence base mixed heart-failure-specific trials with post-hoc cardiovascular-outcome-trial analyses that used less consistent heart-failure definitions.
Canagliflozin efficacy in the review was driven mainly by a post-hoc CANVAS analysis rather than a heart-failure-specific trial, and the authors advised caution.
Many network comparisons had low or very low CINeMA confidence, especially because the network lacked closed loops and was vulnerable to incoherence.
The transitivity assessment identified clinically relevant between-comparison differences in age, sex, ejection fraction, and follow-up.
The active-agent comparative rankings are predominantly indirect rather than supported by direct randomized head-to-head trials.
The authors concluded that SGLT2 inhibitors significantly reduce the composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization in patients with type 2 diabetes and heart failure.
The authors proposed canagliflozin as a possible preferred treatment on the overall network ranking but noted its increased risk of any adverse events.
The authors reported that the heart-failure-specific sensitivity analysis instead ranked sotagliflozin first, followed by empagliflozin and dapagliflozin.
The discussion interpreted reduced heart-failure hospitalization as a probable class effect across SGLT2 inhibitors.
